For reference, T3 Code solves the same setup with one-time pairing links: the server binds `127.0.0.1` only, and `t3 pair --tailscale --tailscale-serve-port 443 --ttl 15m` configures Tailscale Serve and prints a one-time link (plus QR code) to `https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net/…`. Opening it on a new device (phone, laptop) redeems the token once, before it expires, and that device stays paired; the link is useless afterwards. No password, no relay, no SSH tunnel, and the tailnet URL works from any device.

OA could do the same: `openagent pair` → a one-time, short-lived link on the tailnet (or Funnel) URL, accepted alongside the loopback Host check rather than replacing it.

--

Run the dashboard on a tailnet address (Tailscale Serve / Funnel)

**Setup:** OpenAgent 0.38.0 on a headless VM in my tailnet. The dashboard listens on `127.0.0.1:4200`.

**Problem:** the machine sits in my tailnet, and every device I use can reach it over Tailscale with a valid HTTPS certificate. Still, the only working way to open the dashboard is through an external relay server ("door") on a third-party IP, or through an SSH tunnel.

- **Tailscale Serve** (`tailscale serve --bg 4200`, tailnet-only HTTPS at `https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net`): the page loads, but every `/_rpc` call returns `403 unexpected Host header`, so the UI shows "The daemon is not answering". `isExpectedHost()` in `dashboard/rpc-serve.js` only accepts loopback hosts, and nothing configures it.
- **Tailscale Funnel** (public HTTPS through Tailscale): same Host check. On top of that, the door wants its own Let's Encrypt certificate via port 80, and Funnel only exposes 443/8443/10000.

**Request:** a supported way to serve the dashboard behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy on a non-loopback hostname, for example:

1. a setting listing extra allowed hosts (e.g. `allowedHosts: ["<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net"]`), with the same-origin check applied to those hosts, which keeps the DNS-rebinding protection intact;
2. a door mode without its own certificate ("TLS is terminated upstream"), so Funnel or any HTTPS proxy can front it.

Tailscale Serve also passes `Tailscale-User-Login` headers, which could later be used for identity. The main ask is just to let the tailnet URL work.

Opening it on a new device redeems the token once and leaves that device paired. Such paired requests are accepted alongside the loopback Host check, not instead of it. No password, relay or SSH tunnel needed.

Later, perhaps: Tailscale Serve's `Tailscale-User-Login` headers could serve as identity.

Issue: [#2217](https://github.com/openagt/openagent/issues/2217)

# Dashboard on a tailnet address (Tailscale Serve / Funnel)

## TLDR

A dashboard behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy on a non-loopback hostname doesn't work. Behind Tailscale Serve (`tailscale serve --bg 4200`, at `https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net`) the page loads, but every `/_rpc` call gets `403 unexpected Host header`. The cause is `isExpectedHost()` in `dashboard/rpc-serve.js`: it accepts only loopback hosts, and no setting changes that. The UI then shows "The daemon is not answering". Tailscale Funnel hits the same Host check. Its door also can't get its own Let's Encrypt certificate, because Funnel exposes only 443/8443/10000 and not port 80.

Decided (maintainer, in the issue): do it the way T3 Code does, with one-time pairing links.

- OA keeps listening on `127.0.0.1` only and sets up `tailscale serve` itself.
- Pairing is a one-time, short-lived link (and QR code) to the tailnet URL. Opening it on a new device redeems the token once and leaves that device paired; the link is useless afterwards. Paired requests are accepted alongside the loopback Host check, not instead of it.
- Today the link comes from Settings › Devices › Add device; add a command (e.g. `openagent pair`) for headless machines, which have no dashboard to open it from.

Not doing: a setting listing extra allowed hosts. The dashboard trusts whoever reaches it, so on the tailnet anyone the machine is shared with would be the owner in OA.

Later, perhaps: Tailscale Serve's `Tailscale-User-Login` headers could serve as identity.

## Why it matters

Today the only ways to reach a headless machine's dashboard are an external relay on a third-party IP or an SSH tunnel. That holds even when every device is already on the same tailnet with valid HTTPS.
EOF
